title: The hem of his cloak (Mark 5:25–34)
hook: twelve years bleeding, she reaches through the crowd and Jesus stops to find her

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Roman officer said only say the word, and the Mass still says it. Did you carry his two halves, honest and trusting? Day forty.

A crowd, pushing and shoving down a narrow street. Jesus is on his way somewhere urgent: a synagogue leader's daughter is dying, and we'll hear about her tomorrow. Everyone is pressing close. And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody is looking at. For twelve years she's been bleeding. Mark says she had suffered many things from many physicians, spent everything she had, and was no better, but rather worse. Twelve years of appointments, of hope, of bills, of getting worse. She doesn't ask for anything. She doesn't want to be seen. She has one plan, and it's very small. Today: the woman who reached out, and the man who stopped.
screen: `A CROWD ON AN URGENT ERRAND.` → `TWELVE YEARS BLEEDING.` → `ONE VERY SMALL PLAN.`

segments.voice: Her plan, in the Douay-Rheims: "If I shall touch but his garment, I shall be whole." She comes up behind him in the crowd and touches his clothes. Matthew and Luke say the hem, the fringe. Some readers take that as one of the tassels the Law of Moses asks for at the corners of a garment. And at once, Mark says, the bleeding stops, and she feels in her body that she is healed. She could slip away now. Nobody would know. But Jesus stops. He turns around in the crowd and asks: "Who hath touched my garments?" His disciples are baffled. Look at this crowd pressing on you, and you ask who touched you? But he keeps looking around to see who did it. There's a difference between being bumped and being reached for. He felt the reach. And the woman, afraid and trembling, comes forward, falls down before him, and tells him the whole truth, in front of everyone. Why did he stop? He wasn't taking the healing back. He wanted to meet her. Leviticus counts a flow of blood like hers as ritual impurity, a matter of the Temple, not of sin. Mark doesn't say how her neighbors treated her. He says she'd lost her money and her health. Now, in front of the whole crowd, he calls her by a family word: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace." Healed in body, and then named as family in front of everyone. An old tradition gives her a name, but the Gospels don't.
screen: `IF I TOUCH BUT HIS GARMENT.` · `THE HEM — PERHAPS A TASSEL.` · `WHO TOUCHED MY GARMENTS?` · `HE CALLS HER DAUGHTER.` · then, large: `DAUGHTER, THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of help you've needed for a long time and haven't asked for. A doctor's appointment you keep postponing. A friend you haven't told. A counselor, a priest, a parent. Maybe you've been hoping to get the help without anyone seeing. Just name it. Then imagine reaching out, only a little, the way she reached for the hem. If you pray, you can reach for God with it. The bell holds the time.
The hem of his cloak. A woman who reached for it in secret, and a man who stopped to find her. Today's word.
screen: `THE HEM OF HIS CLOAK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he stopped for her. Today, reach out for the help you've needed, even a small first step. And if someone reaches for you, stop. Day forty.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass together with the raising of Jairus's daughter, and some bring long illnesses to prayer and to the anointing of the sick.

original.note: Greek: the edge or tassel of a garment. Matthew and Luke's word for what she touched.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman touches his clothes and is healed.
what it means: she's healed in secret, but he stops the crowd to find her, and calls her daughter in front of everyone.
what a scholar hears: kraspedon, the fringe, perhaps one of the tassels the Law of Moses asks for at a garment's corners.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 5:28, 5:30 and 5:34 given from memory; confirm.
Tassels (tzitzit) as the likely meaning of kraspedon: widely held; confirm phrasing ('many scholars think').
Ritual impurity (Leviticus 15:25–27): the script stresses it concerned Temple purity, not sin, to avoid a negative portrayal of Jewish law. Confirm it is fair and careful.
'An old tradition gives her a name' refers to the Acts of Pilate (Bernice/Veronica); the name is deliberately not given. Confirm.
Mark 5:21–43 is read on the 13th Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year B; confirm.
